subject: tech
title: Computers Around Us
about: Computers hidden all around us (the car, the microwave, the washing machine, traffic lights, the cash register, the library checkout, the thermostat), the workers who use them (doctor, pilot, teacher, farmer, builder, store worker), how life changed from letters, paper maps, film and heavy books to messages, map apps, phone cameras and search, and the idea that computers help but people decide. NC K2-IC-01 (how people lived and worked before and after new technology) and K2-CS-01 (choosing devices for a task). Read it together and spot the hidden computers on your next errand.
tip: On your next errand, count the hidden computers together: the car, the traffic light, the cash register.

cards.q: A car has a small computer inside. What is one job it does?
cards.note: The car's computer checks the engine and lights up the dashboard. The driver still steers.

cards.q: You press the buttons on the microwave and it starts. What counts the seconds?
cards.note: A microwave has a small computer chip. It counts the time and turns the heat off.

cards.q: The washing machine fills, spins and stops all by itself. What tells it the steps?
cards.note: The machine follows a program: fill, wash, rinse, spin. A chip inside runs the steps.

cards.q: Traffic lights on a busy street change together. What keeps them in step?
cards.note: Computers time the lights so cars on one street stop while the others go.

cards.q: At the store, a machine beeps at each thing and adds up the price. What is it?
cards.note: The cash register is a computer. It reads the bar code and adds up the prices.

cards.q: At the library you scan your card and your book. What remembers you have the book?
cards.note: The library's computer keeps a list of who has each book and when it comes back.

cards.q: A little box on the wall keeps the house warm or cool. What is it called?
cards.note: Many thermostats have a small computer. It reads the temperature and turns the heat or air on and off.

cards.q: A doctor looks at a picture of your bones on a screen. What helped make the picture?
cards.note: Doctors use computers to take X-ray pictures and to keep notes about how you are growing.

cards.q: Which worker uses computers to fly a big airplane?
cards.note: The plane's computers show the pilot how high and how fast they are going.

cards.q: Your teacher shows a video on the big board at school. What is the board?
cards.note: Teachers use computers to show lessons, play songs and take attendance.

cards.q: Which worker can use a computer to check if the fields need water?
cards.note: Farmers use computers in tractors and to check the weather and the soil.

cards.q: Before a builder builds a house, what shows the plan on a screen?
cards.note: Builders draw house plans on computers and measure with laser tools.

cards.q: A store worker needs to know how many apples are left. What helps count them?
cards.note: Store computers count what sells so the worker knows what to order.

cards.q: Long ago, people wrote letters on paper and waited days. What do many people send now?
cards.note: A message on a phone or tablet arrives in seconds. A paper letter takes days.

cards.q: Long ago, drivers unfolded big paper maps. What do many drivers use now?
cards.note: A maps app finds the way and talks. Paper maps still work with no battery.

cards.q: Old cameras used film that had to be sent away. What do phone cameras show you?
cards.note: Film cameras made you wait days. A phone camera shows the photo in a blink.

cards.q: Long ago, you looked up facts in big heavy books. What do many people use now?
cards.note: Searching finds facts in seconds. Books are still great, and some things online are not true, so ask a grown-up.

cards.q: Computers help people do jobs faster. Who decides what to do with the help?
cards.note: A computer gives the doctor a picture, but the doctor decides how to help you.
